title: Points of the s-Plane
intro: Every point s = σ + jω of the complex plane is a way of looking at a signal: it multiplies x(t) by a turning arrow that also grows or shrinks, and adds up the result. This page shows what that arrow does, and why the integral converges for some points and not others.

blocks.text: A turning arrow that grows or shrinks
The Laplace transform weights the signal at time $t$ by $e^{-st}$. Write $s = \sigma + j\omega$ and split the exponential in two:

The second factor is a unit-length arrow turning clockwise at $\omega$ radians per second: at time $t$ it points at angle $-\omega t$. The first factor is a real number that sets the arrow's length, and it depends only on $\sigma$. If $\sigma > 0$ the arrow shrinks as time goes on; if $\sigma < 0$ it grows; if $\sigma = 0$ it keeps length 1 and only turns.

Take $s = 0.5 + j2$. At $t = 1$ s the arrow has length $e^{-0.5} = 0.607$ and points at $-2$ rad, which is $-114.6^\circ$. At $t = 2$ s its length is $e^{-1} = 0.368$, and at $t = 4$ s it is $e^{-2} = 0.135$. One full turn takes $2\pi/2 = 3.14$ s, so the arrow draws an inward spiral. Now take $s = -0.5 + j2$: same turning rate, but the length is $e^{0.5} = 1.65$ at $t = 1$ and $e^{1} = 2.72$ at $t = 2$, an outward spiral. A point on the right of the plane gives a shrinking arrow; a point on the left gives a growing one; the imaginary axis gives a pure turn.

If you have read Points of the z-Plane (#/math/z-transform/z-plane), this is the continuous-time version of the same picture. There $z^{-n}$ is sampled at whole numbers of steps and spirals by a fixed factor each step; here $e^{-st}$ is a smooth spiral in time.
Multiplying by the signal and adding up
The transform of $x(t)$ at the point $s$ is the sum, over all time, of the signal's value times that arrow:

Each instant contributes an arrow of length $|x(t)|\,e^{-\sigma t}$ pointing at angle $-\omega t$ (and flipped if $x(t)$ is negative), and $X(s)$ is the total. Pick $\omega$ so the arrow turns in step with a rhythm in the signal and the contributions line up and add; pick it out of step and they point every which way and cancel. That is how the transform measures how much of each frequency is present.
Seen this way, there is a neat fact. Group the exponential differently:

blocks.tex: X(\sigma + j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left[\, x(t)\, e^{-\sigma t} \right] e^{-j\omega t}\, dt

blocks.text: The bracket is the signal after being multiplied by a real exponential, and the rest is the ordinary Fourier transform of that. So a vertical line $\sigma = \text{const}$ in the s-plane is the Fourier transform of $x(t)e^{-\sigma t}$: a choice of $\sigma$ tilts the signal's envelope, and walking up the line in $\omega$ reads off its spectrum. The page The Imaginary Axis and Frequency Response (#/math/laplace-transform/imaginary-axis) uses the line $\sigma = 0$, where there is no tilt.

A worked check: the unit step $u(t)$ has $X(s) = 1/s$. At $s = 0.5 + j2$ that is $1/(0.5 + j2) = 0.118 - 0.471j$, with size $0.485$. Computed the other way, $u(t)e^{-0.5t}$ is the decaying exponential $e^{-0.5t}u(t)$, whose Fourier transform is $1/(0.5 + j\omega)$; at $\omega = 2$ it is the same number.
Why only σ decides convergence

The integral only makes sense if it comes to a finite number. Its size is limited by $\int |x(t)|\,|e^{-st}|\,dt$, and $|e^{-st}| = e^{-\sigma t}$ has no $\omega$ in it. Turning the arrow does not change its length, so whether the total stays finite depends on $\sigma$ alone. The set of good points is therefore a union of vertical lines: a strip, or a half-plane, or the whole plane. It is called the region of convergence, and the next-but-one page, The Region of Convergence (#/math/laplace-transform/region-of-convergence), sorts out which strips can occur.

Take $x(t) = e^{-0.5t}u(t)$. The integrand has size $e^{-0.5t}e^{-\sigma t} = e^{-(0.5+\sigma)t}$. At $\sigma = -0.3$ that is $e^{-0.2t}$, which dies away, and the integral is finite. At $\sigma = -0.7$ it is $e^{+0.2t}$, which grows: cut the integral off at $T = 20$ s and you have 268; at $T = 40$ s, 14 900; it never settles. The boundary is $\sigma = -0.5$, the position of the pole of $X(s) = 1/(s + 0.5)$, and the answer is: convergence for every $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > -0.5$, and the same formula $1/(s+0.5)$ for the value.

A point can have a perfectly good formula and still be outside the region of convergence. $1/(s + 0.5)$ gives a number at $s = -0.7$, namely $-5$, but the integral that defines the transform of $e^{-0.5t}u(t)$ does not converge there, so that number is not the transform. The viewer fades the surface outside the region for exactly this reason.
The plainest surface: a delayed impulse
The simplest signal to read is an impulse at $t = 1$, $x(t) = \delta(t - 1)$. The impulse picks out the value of the integrand at $t = 1$:

blocks.tex: X(s) = \int \delta(t-1)\, e^{-st}\, dt = e^{-s}, \qquad |X(\sigma + j\omega)| = e^{-\sigma}

blocks.text: The arrow is sampled once, at $t = 1$, so $X$ is just the arrow at that instant: length $e^{-\sigma}$, angle $-\omega$. At $\sigma = -1$ the height is $e^{1} = 2.72$; at $\sigma = 1$ it is $e^{-1} = 0.368$; it does not depend on $\omega$ at all. There are no poles and no zeros. There is only a smooth slope across the plane, and the integral converges everywhere, because there is only one instant to add up.

In decibels the slope is a straight ramp: $20\log_{10}e^{-\sigma} = -8.69\,\sigma$ dB. Across the viewer's whole width, $\sigma = -3$ to $\sigma = 3$, the height runs from $+26.1$ dB to $-26.1$ dB, inside the $\pm 30$ dB clip, so you see the whole ramp. The line $\sigma = 0$, the imaginary axis, sits at 0 dB: delaying a signal changes how it looks on every vertical line except that one.

Turn the surface until you look along the $\omega$ direction: it is a straight ramp, higher on the left, lower on the right, crossing the floor-to-top midpoint at $\sigma = 0$. Move Probe frequency ω: the red point slides up the imaginary axis, but the response panel stays a flat line at 0 dB, because $|e^{-j\omega}| = 1$. Then switch Height shows to magnitude: the left of the surface is clipped at the top, since $e^{-\sigma} > 5$ for $\sigma < -1.61$. Finally, change Input signal to the unit impulse: the ramp becomes a flat sheet at 0 dB, and the delay is exactly the tilt.
Problems

blocks.title: Follow an arrow
blocks.text: The point is $s = -0.2 + j3$. How long is the arrow $e^{-st}$ at $t = 5$ s, and which way does it point?
solution: $e^{-st} = e^{0.2t}\,e^{-j3t}$. At $t = 5$ the length is $e^{1} = 2.718$. The angle is $-3 \times 5 = -15$ rad. Adding two full turns, $4\pi = 12.57$, brings it into $(-\pi, \pi]$: $-15 + 12.57 = -2.43$ rad, or $-139.4^\circ$.

blocks.title: Where does it converge?
blocks.text: For $x(t) = e^{3t}u(t)$, for which $s$ does $\int x(t)e^{-st}dt$ converge, and what is the transform?
solution: The integrand has size $e^{3t}e^{-\sigma t} = e^{(3-\sigma)t}$ for $t \ge 0$. It decays only when $\sigma > 3$. There, $\int_0^\infty e^{-(s-3)t}dt = 1/(s-3)$. The pole is at $s = 3$, on the right of the plane, and the region is everything to its right, not including the imaginary axis.
blocks.answer: $X(s) = 1/(s-3)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 3$; the imaginary axis is not in the region.

blocks.title: The delayed impulse
blocks.text: What are $|X|$ and its value in decibels for $\delta(t-1)$ at $s = -2 + j5$?
solution: $X(s) = e^{-s}$, so $|X| = e^{-\sigma} = e^{2} = 7.39$. In decibels, $20\log_{10}7.39 = 17.4$ dB (equivalently $8.69 \times 2$). The $j5$ does not matter.
